newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to abandon striker-replacement legal battle.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to abandon striker-replacement legal battle.

text.p: The Clinton administration has apparently abandoned its legal battle to enforce a presidential order barring the government from contracting with companies that permanently replace striking workers, a Justice Department spokesman said on Monday.

The spokesman, Bert Brandenburg, said the government does not plan to petition the Supreme Court by Monday's deadline to overturn a lower court ruling that struck down President Clinton's executive order of March 8, 1995.
"My understanding is that we have not filed anything today and I've been told that we don't plan to file anything," Brandenberg told Reuters.

Under the order, companies that do more than $100,000 a year of business with the federal government could have had their contracts cancelled and be disqualified from future business if they hired permanent replacements for lawfully striking workers.

But before the order took effect, business groups, led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, persuaded a U.S. District Court judge to temporarily block the administration from enforcing it while they appealed, even though the judge upheld the president's authority to issue the order.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals, however, unanimously overturned the president's order last Feb. 2, ruling that it conflicts with employers' rights under federal labor law to hire permanent replacements. The entire U.S. Appeals Court for the District of Columbia let the panel's ruling stand in May on a 9-2 vote.
